newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-KL shares close down on more currency woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-KL shares close down on more currency woes.

text.p: Malaysian blue-chip shares slid close to four-year lows on Tuesday on sustained concerns over the weakness of the ringgit, before seeing a partial recovery on support from local institutions, dealers and analysts said.
Selling by foreign investors continued, but cash calls on leveraged investors hit an already shaky market, dealers said.
The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed down 4.89 points or 0.54 percent at 897.25.
It had hit a new 1997 low of 884.61 points, but a spurt of local institutional support helped to push it briefly into the black at the 903.12-level.
The last time the Composite Index closed below the 884-level was in November 1995, when it reached 883.96. Its previous closing low was in October 1993, when it hit 859.87.

"There has been some foreign selling here and there, but it has mostly been margin selling," said a dealer at a local bank-backed brokerage. The dealer was referring to calls by banks and brokerage houses on their customers using stocks as collateral to either top up their portfolios with cash or sell off their holdings.
"There's not much pressure from foreigners today," the dealer said.
Continuing uncertainty over the direction of the Malaysian currency remained the main driving force behind the foreign selling, fund managers said.
"Our main worry is the currency, that the ringgit will weaken," said the managing director of a Japanese investment fund in Singapore.
He said he had reduced the fund's exposure to Malaysian equities to "quite close to zero".
Local institutions were seen buying power and telecommunications utilities Tenaga Nasional Bhd, which rose 10 cents, and Telekom Malaysia Bhd, which remained unchanged.
Malayan Banking Bhd closed 30 cents higher at 22.00 ringgit, also on local funds support, said dealers. The three stocks have the heaviest weighting on the index.
Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange executive chairman Nik Mohamad Din Nik Yusoff said the weakness in share prices was due to the weakening ringgit.
"There is nothing wrong with the economy. That is why I urge people to go into the market to buy now," he said earlier on Tuesday.
However, a Reuter poll of 12 research houses showed an average forecast of economic growth slowing to 7.9 percent in 1997, against a growth rate of 8.2 percent in 1996.
"Since interest rates are so high, it is indicating inflationary pressure, and that growth will be sluggish," a fund manager said.

Newly-listed PPB Oil Palm Bhd closed at 2.88 ringgit after debuting at 2.98 ringgit. It was offered at 2.80 ringgit. Analysts said the poor performance of the stock reflected the overall bearishness of the market.
